recommendation_tables.title: Table 4 New recommendations in 2022

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that public-access defibrillation be available at sites where cardiac arrest is more likely to occur.
Prompt CPR by bystanders is recommended at OHCA.
It is recommended to promote community training in basic life support to increase bystander CPR rate and AED use.
Mobile phone-based alerting of basic life support-trained bystander volunteers to assist nearby OHCA victims should be considered.
DC cardioversion is recommended as the first-line treatment for patients presenting with tolerated SMVT provided that the anaesthetic/sedation risk is low.
Optimal medical treatment including ACE-I/ARB/ARNIs, MRAs, beta-blockers, and SGLT2 inhibitors is indicated in all heart failure patients with reduced EF.
Implantation of a cardioverter defibrillator is only recommended in patients who have an expectation of good-quality survival >1 year.
In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated SMVT and known or suspected SHD, intravenous procainamide should be considered.
In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated SMVT in the absence of an established diagnosis, intravenous amiodarone may be considered.

In patients with SMVT or SPVT/VF triggered by a PVC with similar morphology and an indication for ICD, catheter ablation may be considered when an ICD is not available, contraindicated for concurrent medical reasons, or declined by the patient.
The WCD may be considered in the early phase after MI in selected patients.
In patients with CAD and recurrent, symptomatic SMVT, or ICD shocks for SMVT despite chronic amiodarone therapy, catheter ablation is recommended in preference to escalating AAD therapy.

Cardiac stress imaging during physical exercise is recommended in addition to cardiopulmonary exercise test after surgery in patients with anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery with a history of aborted CA.
In SCA survivors with coronary artery spasm, implantation of an ICD should be considered.
ICD therapy should be considered in patients with CAD, NYHA class I, and LVEF ≤30% despite ≥3 months of OMT.
ICD implantation should be considered in patients with CAD, LVEF ≤40% despite ≥3 months of OMT and NSVT, if they are inducible for SMVT by PES.

rows.recommendation: In patients with HCM and recurrent, symptomatic VA, or recurrent symptomatic ICD therapy, AAD treatment should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: LVNC and RCM

rows.recommendation: In patients with an LVNC cardiomyopathy phenotype based on CMR or echocardiography, implantation of an ICD for primary prevention of SCD should be considered to follow DCM/HNDCM recommendations.
An ICD should be considered in patients with light-chain amyloidosis or transthyretin-associated cardiac amyloidosis and haemodynamically not-tolerated VT.

recommendation_tables.title: Neuromuscular diseases

rows.recommendation: Invasive electrophysiological evaluation is recommended in patients with myotonic dystrophy and palpitations or syncope suggestive of VA or surviving a CA.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with myotonic dystrophy and SMVT or aborted CA not caused by BBR-VT.
Invasive electrophysiological evaluation should be considered in patients with myotonic dystrophy and a sudden increase in the PR interval or QRS duration.

Invasive electrophysiological evaluation should be considered in patients with myotonic dystrophy and a PR interval ≥240 ms or QRS duration ≥120 ms or who are older than 40 years and have supraventricular arrhythmias, or who are older than 40 years and have significant LGE on CMR.
In myotonic dystrophy patients without AV conduction delay and a syncope highly suspicious for VA, ICD implantation should be considered.
In myotonic dystrophy patients with palpitations highly suspicious for VA and induction of a non-BBR-VT, ICD implantation should be considered.
In patients with limb–girdle type 1B or Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophies and indication for pacing, ICD implantation should be considered.
Implantation of an ICD may be considered in patients with Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy and significant LGE at CMR.
Implantation of an ICD over a permanent pacemaker may be considered in myotonic dystrophy patients with additional risk factors¶ for VA and SCD.

In patients with myotonic dystrophy, serial electrophysiological evaluation of AV conduction and arrhythmia induction is not recommended without arrhythmia suspicion or progression of ECG conduction disorders.

recommendation_tables.title: Inflammatory diseases

rows.recommendation: In patients with haemodynamically not-tolerated sustained VT or VF during the acute phase of myocarditis, ICD implantation before hospital discharge should be considered.
In post-myocarditis patients with recurrent, symptomatic VT, AAD treatment should be considered.

Catheter ablation, performed in specialized centres, should be considered in post-myocarditis patients with recurrent, symptomatic SMVT, or ICD shocks for SMVT in whom AADs are ineffective, not tolerated, or not desired.
In patients with haemodynamically tolerated SMVT occurring in the chronic phase of myocarditis, ICD implantation should be considered.
In patients with cardiac sarcoidosis who have an LVEF >35% but significant LGE at CMR after resolution of acute inflammation, ICD implantation should be considered.
In patients with cardiac sarcoidosis who have an LVEF 35–50% and minor LGE at CMR, after resolution of acute inflammation, PES for risk stratification should be considered.
In patients with cardiac sarcoidosis, LVEF 35–50%, and inducible SMVT at PES, ICD implantation should be considered.
In patients with cardiac sarcoidosis and recurrent, symptomatic VA, AAD treatment should be considered.
Amiodarone should be considered to reduce arrhythmia burden in patients with Chagas’ cardiomyopathy who present with symptomatic PVCs or VT.

In patients with Chagas’ cardiomyopathy and recurrent, symptomatic SMVT, or ICD shocks for SMVT in whom AADs are ineffective, contraindicated, or not tolerated, catheter ablation in specialized centres should be considered.

In patients with haemodynamically well-tolerated SMVT occurring in the chronic phase of myocarditis, preserved LV function and a limited scar amenable to ablation, catheter ablation may be considered as an alternative to ICD therapy, after discussion with the patient and provided that established endpoints have been reached.

Catheter ablation, in specialized centres, may be considered in cardiac sarcoidosis ICD recipients with recurrent, symptomatic SMVT, or ICD shocks for SMVT, in whom AADs are ineffective, contraindicated, or not tolerated.

recommendation_tables.title: Congenital heart disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with CHD presenting with sustained VAs, evaluation for residual lesions or new structural abnormalities is recommended.

In selected patients with CHD (including atrial baffle repair for transposition of the great arteries, Fontan operation, and Ebstein anomaly) presenting with CA, evaluation and treatment of SVT with rapid ventricular conduction should be considered.

In patients with repaired TOF undergoing surgical or transcutaneous pulmonary valve replacement, pre-operative catheter mapping and transection of VT-related anatomical isthmuses before or during the intervention may be considered.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents guideline recommendations for management of various inherited arrhythmia syndromes, including Idiopathic VF, Long QT syndrome, Andersen–Tawil syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and Early repolarization syndrome.

rows.recommendation: In patients with repaired TOF with a preserved biventricular function and symptomatic SMVT, catheter ablation or concomitant surgical ablation performed in specialized centres may be considered as an alternative to ICD therapy.

It is recommended that idiopathic VF is diagnosed in a SCA survivor, preferably with documentation of VF, after exclusion of an underlying structural, channelopathic, metabolic, or toxicological aetiology.
Isoproterenol infusion, verapamil, or quinidine for acute treatment of an electrical storm or recurrent ICD discharges should be considered in idiopathic VF.
Quinidine should be considered for chronic therapy to suppress an electrical storm or recurrent ICD discharges in idiopathic VF.
Clinical testing (history, ECG, and high precordial lead ECG, exercise test, echocardiogram) of first-degree family members of idiopathic VF patients may be considered.
In idiopathic VF patients, genetic testing of genes related to channelopathy and cardiomyopathy may be considered.
In patients with clinically diagnosed LQTS, genetic testing, and genetic counselling are recommended.
Beta-blockers, ideally non-selective beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol), are recommended in LQTS patients with documented QT interval prolongation, to reduce risk of arrhythmic events.
Mexiletine is indicated in LQT3 patients with a prolonged QT interval.
In LQTS, it should be considered to calculate the arrhythmic risk before initiation of therapy based on the genotype and the duration of QTc interval.

ICD implantation may be considered in asymptomatic LQTS patients with high-risk profile (according to the 1-2-3 LQTS Risk calculator) in addition to genotype-specific medical therapies (mexiletine in LQT3 patients).
Routine diagnostic testing with epinephrine challenge is not recommended in LQTS.
Genetic testing is recommended in patients with suspected Andersen–Tawil syndrome.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome after aborted CA or not-tolerated sustained VT.

Andersen–Tawil syndrome should be considered in patients without SHD who present with at least two of the following: • Prominent U waves with or without prolongation of the QT interval • Bidirectional and/or polymorphic PVCs/VT • Dysmorphic features • Periodic paralysis • KCNJ2 pathogenic loss of function mutation.
Beta-blockers and/or flecainide with or without acetazolamide should be considered in patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome to treat VA.
An ILR should be considered in patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome and unexplained syncope.
ICD implantation may be considered in patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome who have a history of unexplained syncope or suffer from tolerated sustained VT.
Genetic testing for SCN5A gene is recommended for probands with BrS.

BrS should be considered in patients with no other heart disease and induced type 1 Brugada pattern who have at least one of the following: • Arrhythmic syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration • A family history of BrS • A family history of SD (<45 years old) with a negative autopsy and circumstance suspicious for BrS.
Implantation of a loop recorder should be considered in BrS patients with an unexplained syncope.
BrS may be considered as a diagnosis in patients with no other heart disease who exhibit an induced type 1 Brugada ECG.
PES may be considered in asymptomatic patients with a spontaneous type I BrS ECG.
Sodium channel blocker test is not recommended in patients with a prior type I Brugada pattern.
Catheter ablation in asymptomatic BrS patients is not recommended.
It is recommended that the ERP is diagnosed as J-point elevation of ≥1 mm in two adjacent inferior and/or lateral ECG leads.
It is recommended that the ERS is diagnosed in a patient resuscitated from unexplained VF/PVT in the presence of ERP.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with a diagnosis of ERS who have survived a CA.
In a SCD victim with a negative autopsy and medical chart review, and an ante-mortem ECG demonstrating the ERP, the diagnosis of ERS should be considered.
First-degree relatives of ERS patients should be considered for clinical evaluation for ERP with additional high-risk features.i
ILR should be considered in individuals with ERP and at least one risk featurek or arrhythmic syncope.
Isoproterenol infusion should be considered for ERS patients with electrical storm.
Quinidine in addition to an ICD should be considered for recurrent VF in ERS patients.
PVC ablation should be considered in ERS patients with recurrent VF episodes triggered by a similar PVC non-responsive to medical treatment.
Genetic testing in ERS patients may be considered.
ICD implantation or quinidine may be considered in individuals with ERP and arrhythmic syncope and additional risk features.k

recommendation_tables.title: CPVT

rows.recommendation: Genetic testing and genetic counselling are indicated in patients with clinical suspicion or clinical diagnosis of CPVT.
Beta-blockers, ideally non-selective (nadolol or propranolol) are recommended in all patients with a clinical diagnosis of CPVT.

recommendation_tables.title: Short QT syndrome

rows.recommendation: Genetic testing is indicated in patients diagnosed with SQTS.
SQTS should be considered in the presence of a QTc ≤320 ms.
SQTS should be considered in the presence of a QTc ≥320 ms and ≤360 ms and arrhythmic syncope.
ILR should be considered in young SQTS patients.
ICD implantation should be considered in SQTS patients with arrhythmic syncope.
SQTS may be considered in the presence of a QTc ≥320 ms and ≤360 ms and a family history of SD at age <40 years.
Quinidine may be considered in (a) SQTS patients who qualify for an ICD but present a contraindication to the ICD or refuse it, and (b) asymptomatic SQTS patients and a family history of SCD.
Isoproterenol may be considered in SQTS patients with an electrical storm.

recommendation_tables.title: Selected populations

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that athletes diagnosed with a cardiovascular disease associated with SCD are managed according to current guidelines for sports eligibility.
Continuation of beta-blockers should be considered during pregnancy in women with ARVC.
Oral metoprolol, propranolol, or verapamil should be considered for long-term management of idiopathic sustained VT during pregnancy.

Catheter ablation using non-fluoroscopic mapping systems should be considered, preferably after the first trimester, in women with highly symptomatic recurrent SMVT refractory or who are intolerant to AADs.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion of sudden cardiac death (SCD) epidemiology, noting incidence increases with age, gender and ethnic differences, and that most SCD in sports is recreational. Section 4.2 outlines age‐specific causes: in younger individuals primary electrical diseases, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis predominate, while in older populations chronic structural coronary and non‐ischemic diseases account for over half of cases. Section 4.3 describes population versus individual risk prediction, highlighting genetic predisposition to SCD. Section 4.4 reviews existing SCD risk calculators, their development, validation metrics, and limitations. Section 4.5 introduces public basic life support and automated external defibrillator access, with text cut off mid‐discussion.

content.narrative_summary: The page includes narrative text discussing resuscitative interventions prior to emergency medical system arrival as key elements to improve survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients. It notes that bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and use of public automated external defibrillators (AEDs) improve neurological and functional outcomes and survival. The text supports increased availability of public access defibrillators, community training in basic life support (preferably initiated in childhood and repetitive), and dispatch of basic life support–trained volunteers via mobile app networks to raise bystander-initiated CPR rates, reduce the resuscitation-free interval, and improve outcomes.

content.narrative_summary: The text discusses the importance of diagnosing the underlying aetiology of idiopathic ventricular tachycardia (VT). Initial evaluation should include clinical and family history, 12-lead ECG, and echocardiography, with recording of the VT ECG to identify site of origin. Specific morphologies (e.g., RVOT or fascicular origin) without structural heart disease (SHD) suggest idiopathic VT. Atypical ECG features or presentations warrant further evaluation with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for SHD. Bundle branch re-entrant VT (BBR-VT) may indicate conduction impairment in conditions like dilated cardiomyopathy. If coronary artery disease (CAD) is suspected, coronary angiography (CAG) is used. When non-invasive tests are inconclusive, electroanatomical mapping, programmed electrical stimulation, and guided biopsy (e.g., for ARVC or inflammatory diseases) along with PET-CT, serology, and tissue biopsy may be employed.

content.narrative_summary: An algorithm for evaluation of sudden death (SD) victims is presented in Figure 7. Potential genetic cardiac disease is identified in 25–49% of young SD cases (<50 years), and expert autopsy by a cardiac pathologist alters the initial diagnosis in 41%, identifying inherited conditions such as HCM, DCM, ARVC, and premature CAD. Toxicology screening reveals drug overdose or polypharmacy in 31–56% of young SD cases; in autopsy-negative cases with negative toxicology, the term SADS may be applied and primary electrical diseases considered. Retention of tissue for DNA extraction is important, with yields as high as one out of three. Clinical evaluation of first-degree relatives is recommended if the cause of death after autopsy is unknown or suspected to be inherited. Reported combined diagnostic yield of clinical and genetic evaluation is 18–53%, and post-mortem genetic testing targeted to the cause of death identifies mutations in around one-third of cases.

rows.recommendation: In SCA survivors, brain/chest CT scan should be considered when patient characteristics, ECG, and echocardiography are not consistent with a cardiac cause.
In SCA survivors, collection of blood samples at presentation is recommended for potential toxicology and genetic testing.
Retrieval of recordings from CIEDs and wearable monitors is recommended for all SCA survivors.
In SCA survivors, repeated 12-lead ECGs during stable rhythm (including high precordial lead ECG), as well as continuous cardiac monitoring, are recommended.
Echocardiography is recommended for evaluation of cardiac structure and function in all SCA survivors.
Coronary imaging and CMR with LGE are recommended for evaluation of cardiac structure and function in all SCA survivors without a clear underlying cause.
Sodium channel blocker test and exercise testing is recommended in SCA survivors without a clear underlying cause.
In SCA survivors, ergonovine, acetylcholine, or hyperventilation testing may be considered for the diagnosis of coronary vasospasm.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 7 — Recommendations for evaluation of relatives of sudden arrhythmic death syndrome decedents

rows.recommendation:
Familial evaluation of SADS decedents is recommended:
• for first-degree relatives
• for relatives who must carry a mutation based on analysis of the family history
• for relatives with suspicious symptoms
• when the decedent’s age is < 50 years, or if there is other circumstantial data or family history to suggest heritable disease.
Familial evaluation of SADS decedents is recommended to include genetic testing when post-mortem genetic testing in a SADS decedent detects a pathogenic mutation.

Baseline familial evaluation of SADS decedents is recommended to include taking a medical history and performing physical examination, standard and high precordial lead ECG, echocardiography, and exercise testing.
In SADS families without a diagnosis after clinical evaluation, follow-up is recommended for children of decedents until they reach adulthood.

Pharmacological testing with a sodium channel blocker should be considered in relatives of SADS decedents who are 16 years or older when baseline testing and/or proband findings increase the suspicion of BrS.
Ambulatory cardiac rhythm monitoring and CMR may be considered in relatives of SADS decedents.

Pharmacological testing including epinephrine challenge (if exercise testing is impractical) and sodium channel blocker challenge may be considered in first-degree relatives of SADS decedents with normal baseline testing.

In SADS families without a diagnosis after clinical evaluation, follow-up is not recommended for asymptomatic adults who can be discharged with advice to return if they develop symptoms or if the family history changes.

section_headings: 6.1.2. Acute management of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the acute management of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (SMVT). It recommends synchronized cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable patients, unsynchronized shock if synchronization is not possible, and highlights the role of 12-lead ECG documentation. Intravenous adenosine may terminate specific VT subtypes and support triggered activity mechanisms. Pre-excited atrial fibrillation can mimic VT. Drugs that slow AV conduction should be avoided, and prompt termination of SMVT is advised due to rapid deterioration risk.

rows.recommendation: Withdrawal of offending agents is recommended whenever drug-induced VAs are suspected.
Investigation for reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte imbalances, ischaemia, hypoxaemia, fever) is recommended in patients with VA.
Despite a possible correctable cause for the presenting VA, the need for ICD implantation should be considered based on an individual evaluation of the risk of subsequent VA/SCD.

content.narrative_summary: The text reviews strategies for terminating ventricular tachycardia (VT), including electrical cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs such as procainamide and amiodarone, and pacing techniques. It describes the PROCAMIO trial results favoring procainamide over amiodarone with fewer adverse cardiac events, notes contraindications for procainamide in severe heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, and end-stage renal disease, and mentions other AADs (ajmaline, sotalol, flecainide). Manual overdrive pacing in ICD patients is discussed. For idiopathic VT, beta-blockers (for RVOT VT) or verapamil (for fascicular VT) are recommended, with cautions against IV verapamil when VT etiology is uncertain. It emphasizes comprehensive evaluation of patients with sustained monomorphic VT when underlying cardiac disease is unknown. content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses the management of patients presenting with electrical storm or recurrent ventricular arrhythmias. Initial hemodynamic instability warrants advanced life support and correction of reversible causes. Subsequent management is tailored to the type of ventricular arrhythmia and underlying aetiology, often requiring a combined strategy of ICD reprogramming, anti-arrhythmic drug therapy, sedation, catheter ablation, autonomic modulation, and mechanical circulatory support. Elevated sympathetic tone is addressed with sedation for patients with recurrent ICD shocks. First-line pharmacologic therapy includes non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) combined with amiodarone, with landiolol considered for recurrent, amiodarone-resistant, hemodynamically intolerant VTs. Anti-arrhythmic agents such as procainamide, lidocaine, or quinidine are selected based on VA type and aetiology. Intractable electrical storm despite available AADs and multiple shocks merits deep sedation/intubation and mechanical ventilation. When beta-blockers are insufficient or not tolerated, percutaneous ganglionic blockade, thoracic epidural anesthesia, or left cardiac sympathetic denervation may be used for autonomic modulation. The most common arrhythmia in structural heart disease is SMVT, which is amenable to catheter ablation; successful ablation reduces VT recurrence, electrical storm, and improves long-term survival. In incessant slow monomorphic VT, catheter ablation is preferred over further AAD therapy.

content.narrative_summary: Optimal medical treatment of the underlying cardiac disease, including maximal tolerated doses of heart failure medications, is mandatory. In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the 2021 ESC Guidelines recommend angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I)/angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB)/angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), beta-blockers, and sodium–glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors to reduce mortality due to heart failure and sudden cardiac death.

rows.recommendation: In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated idiopathic VT, treatment with intravenous beta-blocker (RVOT VT) or verapamil (fascicular VT) is recommended.
In patients presenting with a regular haemodynamically tolerated wide QRS complex tachycardia suspected for SVT, administration of adenosine or vagal manoeuvres should be considered.
In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated SMVT and known or suspected SHD, intravenous procainamide should be considered.
In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated SMVT in the absence of an established diagnosis, intravenous amiodarone may be considered.
In patients presenting with a haemodynamically tolerated SMVT in the absence of significant SHD, flecainide, ajmaline, or sotalol may be considered.
Intravenous verapamil is not recommended in broad QRS complex tachycardia of unknown mechanism.
Mild to moderate sedation is recommended in patients with electrical storm to alleviate psychological distress and reduce sympathetic tone.
Antiarrhythmic therapy with beta-blockers (non-selective preferred) in combination with intravenous amiodarone is recommended in patients with SHD and electrical storm unless contraindicated.
Intravenous magnesium with supplementation of potassium is recommended in patients with TdP.
Isoproterenol or transvenous pacing to increase heart rate is recommended in patients with acquired LQT syndrome and recurrent TdP despite correction of precipitating conditions and magnesium.
Catheter ablation is recommended in patients presenting with incessant VT or electrical storm due to SMVT refractory to AADs.
Deep sedation/intubation should be considered in patients with an intractable electrical storm refractory to drug treatment.
Catheter ablation should be considered in patients with recurrent episodes of PVT/VT triggered by a similar PVC, non-responsive to medical treatment or coronary revascularization.
Quinidine may be considered in patients with CAD and electrical storm due to recurrent PVT when other AAD therapy fails.

section_headings: 7.1.1.3.4 Management of patients with haemodynamically tolerated ventricular tachycardia and preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction
content.narrative_summary: This section continues discussion of ICD therapy and catheter ablation for ventricular tachycardia in post-MI patients. A meta-analysis demonstrated a 28% mortality reduction (HR 0.72; P=0.0006) with ICDs, primarily by reducing arrhythmic death (HR 0.50; P<0.0001), translating to 4.4 months survival benefit over 6 years. Approximately 80% of patients had CAD, and those with well-tolerated SMVT were excluded from secondary prevention trials. A retrospective study in patients with LVEF >30% and well-tolerated SMVT compared catheter ablation (first-line in 166 patients, mean LVEF 50%) to ICD implantation (378 controls) over 32 months, showing no difference in overall mortality. The data support consideration of ICD implantation or ablation in centres experienced in haemodynamically tolerated SMVT, noting secondary prevention ICD trials did not demonstrate survival benefit in LVEF ≥35%.

section_headings: Recommendation Table 26 — Recommendations for the management of patients with idiopathic premature ventricular complexes/ventricular tachycardia
content.narrative_summary: PVC-induced cardiomyopathy is a recognized reversible cause of LV dysfunction in patients without structural heart disease. Evaluation relies on medical/family history, 12-lead ECG, Holter monitoring and echocardiography; CMR may be considered even with a normal echo. A PVC burden ≥10% is the minimal threshold for PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, with risk rising further when burden exceeds 20%. In patients with <10% burden, other causes should be evaluated. Frequent PVCs may also worsen LV function in structural heart disease, and CMR with late gadolinium enhancement helps distinguish PVC-induced from underlying disease. Diagnosis is confirmed only after LVEF normalization following PVC suppression. Catheter ablation is highly effective (75–90% success) and first-line for PVC-induced cardiomyopathy; outcomes depend on PVC origin and morphology. Anti-arrhythmic medications, including amiodarone and flecainide, can reduce PVC burden and improve LVEF; sodium channel blockers are also effective.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). ARVC predominantly involves the right ventricle; 2010 Task Force criteria use a multiparametric approach without CMR tissue characterization, yet RV fatty infiltration and LV LGE may be present before major imaging criteria are met. Wall motion and signal abnormalities on CMR improve diagnostic accuracy, and recognition of biventricular or left-dominant forms has led to the term ‘arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.’ High-intensity exercise restriction is advised to reduce VA risk, though benefits in asymptomatic mutation carriers are unproven; high-dose isoprenaline can provoke PVT in >90% of ARVC patients, and the role of beta-blockers remains unclear. ARVC is inherited, with fibrofatty myocardial replacement, prevalence 1:1 000–1:5 000, male predominance, and younger onset of SCD/VT (median age 23 vs. 36 for SMVT). Genetic testing for desmosomal mutations is a major diagnostic criterion; compound/digenic mutations occur in 4–16% of probands, and penetrance in first-degree relatives is 28–58%, supporting family screening.

content.narrative_summary: This section discusses inflammatory cardiomyopathies, particularly myocarditis, characterized by myocardial inflammation as a primary cause of cardiac damage. Myocarditis diagnosis relies on clinical presentation (ranging from subtle symptoms to fulminant heart failure, AV block, and SCD), histological and immunohistochemical criteria on endomyocardial biopsy, and PCR for viral genomes. Management of suspected or confirmed acute myocarditis with life-threatening presentations requires referral to specialized centres capable of catheterization, biopsies, mechanical circulatory support, and arrhythmia management. Sustained ventricular arrhythmias may occur in acute myocarditis, with varying reported incidences; giant cell myocarditis carries especially high risk. Treatment of arrhythmias follows standard principles, including AADs (e.g., amiodarone, beta-blockers), ICD implantation, and catheter ablation as indicated.

content.narrative_summary: This section defines cardiac sarcoidosis as a multisystem inflammatory disease with genetic predisposition, characterized by T-lymphocyte–driven granulomas leading to myocardial scarring. Although lung involvement is most common, about 5% of patients have clinical cardiac involvement and many more have subclinical disease detected by advanced imaging. Diagnosis can mimic ARVC, and electroanatomical mapping may help distinguish isolated cardiac sarcoidosis. Three main cardiac manifestations are LV dysfunction, AV conduction abnormalities, and ventricular arrhythmias. Adverse prognostic factors include LVEF <35%, high-degree AV block, and scar on CMR or PET-CT. Studies in biopsy-proven extracardiac sarcoidosis demonstrate that reduced LVEF, VT inducibility, and abnormal CMR/PET predict arrhythmic events and SCD risk. Data support ICD use for primary prevention in patients with LVEF ≤35% and other high-risk features.

content.narrative_summary: Valvular heart disease predisposes to sudden cardiac death both before and after surgical or transcatheter interventions, with reported SCD rates ranging from 15–60% depending on valve pathology. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is associated with about 5.6% SCD at 22-month follow-up. Mitral valve prolapse–related arrhythmic risk (including SMVT and juvenile SCD) has been linked to anatomical features (mitral annular disjunction, fibrosis) and ECG abnormalities, though robust risk-stratification recommendations are lacking.

content.narrative_summary: Advances in surgical repair and medical treatment have improved long-term prognosis of children born with congenital heart disease (CHD), with more than 90% now surviving to adulthood and a steadily increasing prevalence of adult CHD. Fewer patients die from peri-operative events and early heart failure, making sudden cardiac death (SCD) a leading cause of death in adults with repaired CHD. A combination of surgical incisions, myocardial scar and residual or new anatomical abnormalities form the substrate for ventricular arrhythmias (VAs). Risk stratification for sudden cardiac death in CHD is challenging due to mixed patient populations, lack of randomized trials and small observational studies. A left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35% remains the standard criterion for primary prevention ICD selection in patients with biventricular physiology and systemic RVs. In patients with unexplained syncope or severe arrhythmia symptoms, programmed electrical stimulation (PES) may be considered. Electrophysiological evaluation may refine risk stratification in asymptomatic tetralogy of Fallot patients. Surgical era and techniques affect VA substrate and occurrence. Use of a transannular patch in TOF is associated with lower VA risk. Primary prevention ICD therapy in patients with single or systemic RVs requires individualized consideration of disease and patient factors.

section_headings: 7.2.2. Long QT syndrome (including acquired long QT syndrome)
content.narrative_summary: This section describes long QT syndrome (LQTS), characterized by prolonged QT interval and adrenergic‐triggered ventricular arrhythmias, with a mean presentation age of 14 years and variable rates of sudden cardiac death. It reviews genetic findings: rare variants in 17 genes have been associated but only KCNQ1, KCNH2, and SCN5A are undisputed causes of LQT1‐3, accounting for most genotyped cases. LQTS subtypes are grouped by inheritance and extracardiac features, including Andersen–Tawil (LQT7), Timothy (LQT8), and autosomal‐recessive Jervell and Lange–Nielsen syndromes. Diagnostic criteria include QTc thresholds (≥480 ms or risk score >3; ≥460 ms with syncope or cardiac arrest) and proposed QT adjustment formulas for patients with broad QRS complexes. The narrative ends mid‐sentence.

content.narrative_summary: Andersen–Tawil syndrome Type 1 (LQT7) is a rare disorder characterized by frequent ventricular arrhythmias, dysmorphologies and periodic paralysis. KCNJ2 loss-of-function mutations decrease IK1, increasing U-wave amplitude rather than QT prolongation. Syncope or documented VT carries risk of life-threatening VA, with a 5-year probability of 7.9%. In patients with sustained haemodynamic-ally not-tolerated VT or cardiac arrest an ICD is recommended. Flecainide and/or beta-blockers reduce VA, whereas amiodarone may be proarrhythmic and should only be used with ICD. In those with syncope, ICD or ILR should be considered. Brugada syndrome type 1 ECG shows J-point elevation ≥2 mV with coved ST elevation and T-wave inversion in right precordial leads. It may be spontaneous or drug/fever-induced, and phenocopies must be excluded. BrS patients without other heart disease have low prevalence but high risk of arrhythmia; SCN5A is the primary gene for clinical testing. Triggers include psychotropic drugs, anaesthetics, cocaine, alcohol and fever. ICD implantation is indicated in symptomatic BrS survivors of CA or documented VF/VT. Up to one-third of patients present with syncope; unexplained syncope carries a fourfold higher risk. ILR studies detect arrhythmias in 20–36% of BrS patients with syncope. Asymptomatic patients represent most newly diagnosed BrS, but their risk stratification remains challenging.

content.narrative_summary: The text discusses management of ventricular arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome, noting that inducibility of sustained ventricular arrhythmias during electrophysiological studies predicts higher risk but is only clinically actionable in asymptomatic patients with spontaneous type 1 Brugada ECG. Electrophysiological mapping identifies an arrhythmogenic fibrotic substrate in the epicardial RVOT responsible for ST‐segment elevation and VF, and ablation of these areas can suppress VF and normalize the ECG in most patients. content.narrative_summary: Early repolarization syndrome (ERS) is diagnosed in patients resuscitated from PVT or VF without structural heart disease who exhibit J-point elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 adjacent inferior and/or lateral leads (ERP). Although often benign and present in ~5.8% of adults—especially young males and athletes—ERP is overrepresented in relatives of SADS cases and CA survivors. Genetic testing yields low diagnostic utility. High-risk ECG features include J-waves ≥2 mm, dynamic J-point changes >0.1 mV, and horizontal/descending ST-segment patterns, which are associated with arrhythmic risk. Management of electrical storms may involve isoproterenol infusion, AADs (e.g., cilostazol, milrinone), and ablation of PVC triggers (Purkinje-system focus). Data on risk stratification without prior CA are limited; follow-up with ILR is recommended in asymptomatic ERP, and ICD implantation or quinidine may be considered in high-risk ERP with strong family history of juvenile SD.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative describes the clinical manifestations, diagnostic evaluation, and management of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT). CPVT typically presents in the first decade of life with exercise- or emotion-induced arrhythmias and often normal resting ECG and echocardiogram. Exercise stress testing is critical for diagnosis, with bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia elicited. Genetic mutations can support diagnosis when stress testing is not feasible. First-line therapy includes exercise restriction and non-selective beta-blockers (e.g., nadolol, propranolol), with flecainide added if arrhythmias persist. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are indicated for survivors of cardiac arrest and considered for recurrent ventricular arrhythmias despite medical therapy. Left cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) may be used as adjunctive therapy when pharmacological treatment is ineffective.

Quinidine may be considered in (a) SQTS patients who qualify for an ICD but present a contraindication to the ICD or refuse it, and (b) asymptomatic SQTS patients and a family history of SCD.

section_headings: 8.1.1. Electrocardioversion and implantable cardioverter defibrillator therapy in pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Pregnancy and the post-partum period carry heightened risk of ventricular arrhythmias and peri-partum cardiomyopathy (PPCM). New-onset VT during pregnancy and recurrent VT in patients with previous VT and structural heart disease are discussed. PPCM should be excluded in late pregnancy and early post-partum. Genetic factors, especially titin-truncating variants, may underlie up to 20% of PPCM cases. Electrical cardioversion is safe throughout pregnancy; if an ICD is indicated, implantation is advised after 8 weeks gestation with radiation protection and echocardiographic or 3D mapping guidance. Pharmacological treatment should follow non-pregnant protocols, avoiding contraindicated drugs, with dose started after the first trimester at the lowest effective dose. Catheter ablation for symptomatic tachyarrhythmias is preferred before pregnancy or using electroanatomical mapping in the second trimester if necessary.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 47 — Recommendations for the prevention of sudden cardiac death and management of ventricular arrhythmia during pregnancy

rows.recommendation: During pregnancy, electrical cardioversion is recommended for sustained VT.
For acute conversion of haemodynamically tolerated SMVT during pregnancy, a beta-blocker, sotalol, flecainide, procainamide, or overdrive ventricular pacing should be considered.
If ICD implantation is indicated during pregnancy, implantation is recommended with optimal radiation protection.
Continuation of beta-blockers is recommended during pregnancy and post-partum in women with LQTS or CPVT.
Continuation of beta-blockers should be considered during pregnancy in women with ARVC.
Oral metoprolol, propranolol, or verapamil should be considered for long-term management of idiopathic sustained VT during pregnancy.

Catheter ablation using non-fluoroscopic mapping systems should be considered, preferably after the first trimester, in women with highly symptomatic recurrent SMVT refractory or who are intolerant to AADs.

content.narrative_summary: Section 8.2 reviews the elevated risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients listed for or after heart transplantation, noting that implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) may offer survival benefit and that wearable cardioverter defibrillators (WCDs) might be alternatives in select waiting-list patients. Section 8.3 summarizes the incidence of SCD in athletes by age group, describes the effectiveness and limitations of pre-participation cardiovascular screening (history, examination, ECG, and selective imaging), and emphasizes the need for targeted evaluation, AED availability, and CPR training.

section_headings: 8.5. Prevention of sudden cardiac death in the elderly
content.narrative_summary: Section 8.4 reviews Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, identifying AV re-entry tachycardia (80 %) and AF (20–30 %) as the most common arrhythmias, and noting a SCD risk of 0.9–2.4 per 1000 person-years. Catheter ablation is recommended for symptomatic patients and for risk stratification or ablation in asymptomatic patients with high-risk pathways. In children under 8 years, risk stratification is not recommended. Section 8.5 discusses prevention of SCD in the elderly, emphasizing that advanced age (>75 years) is associated with reduced ICD benefit and non-arrhythmic mortality, with contemporary data supporting a personalized, comorbidity-based approach to ICD implantation.

content.title: Gaps in evidence
content.narrative_summary: The page outlines remaining knowledge gaps across various cardiovascular conditions. Under section 9.3 it briefly reviews primary electrical disease management preferences (e.g., beta-blockers in LQTS and CPVT, Brugada testing, exclusion of structural causes in idiopathic VF). Section 10 details evidence gaps: 10.1 highlights the need for accurate SCD screening, timing of prognostic tests, assessment of variants of uncertain significance, and polygenic risk scores; 10.2 notes unknowns around long-term safety and efficacy of S-ICDs, preventive ICD use in SHD, VT mapping techniques, and LVAD-supported ICD implantation; 10.3–10.8 summarize a lack of definitive data on catheter ablation or drugs in idiopathic PVCs/VT, risk stratification and ICD roles in chronic CAD, sarcoidosis/HCM/DCM risk with LGE-CMR or PES, VA/SCD risk in MVP and CHD, and the need for robust data on prophylactic ICD use and gene-specific therapy in LQTS.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for genetic testing

rows.recommendation: Genetic testing is recommended when a condition is diagnosed in a living or deceased individual with a likely genetic basis and a risk of VA and SCD.
When a putative causative variant is first identified, evaluation for pathogenicity is recommended using an internationally accepted framework.

When a Class IV or Class V variant has been identified in a living or deceased individual with a condition that carries a risk of VA and SCD, genetic testing of first-degree and symptomatic relatives and obligate carriers is recommended.
It is recommended that genetic testing and counselling on its potential consequences should be undertaken by an expert multidisciplinary team.
It is recommended that Class III variants (of uncertain significance) and Class IV variants should be evaluated for segregation in families where possible, and the variant re-evaluated periodically.
It is not recommended to undertake genetic testing in index patients with insufficient evidence of a genetic disease.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for evaluation of patients presenting with newly documented ventricular arrhythmia

rows.recommendation: In patients with newly documented VA (frequent PVCs, NSVT, SMVT), a baseline 12-lead ECG, recording of the VA on 12-lead ECG, whenever possible, and an echocardiogram are recommended as first-line evaluation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for evaluation of sudden cardiac arrest survivors

rows.recommendation: The investigation of a SCA survivor without obvious extra-cardiac cause is recommended to be overseen by a multidisciplinary team.
In electrically unstable patients after SCA, with suspicion of ongoing myocardial ischaemia, a coronary angiogram is indicated.
In SCA survivors, collection of blood samples at presentation is recommended for potential toxicology and genetic testing.
Retrieval of recordings from CIEDs and wearable monitors is recommended for all SCA survivors.
In SCA survivors, repeated 12-lead ECGs during stable rhythm (including high precordial lead ECG) as well as continuous cardiac monitoring are recommended.
Echocardiography is recommended for evaluation of cardiac structure and function in all SCA survivors.
Coronary imaging and CMR with LGE are recommended for evaluation of cardiac structure and function in all SCA survivors without a clear underlying cause.
Sodium channel blocker test and exercise testing is recommended in SCA survivors without a clear underlying cause.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for evaluation of sudden death victims

rows.recommendation: Investigation of unexpected SD, especially in case of suspicion of inherited disease, should be made a public health priority.
In cases of SD, it is recommended to collect a detailed description of circumstances of death, symptoms prior to death, the family history, and to review prior medical files.
A comprehensive autopsy is recommended, ideally, in all cases of unexpected SD, and always in those under 50 years of age.
In cases of SCD, it is recommended to retain samples suitable for DNA extraction and consult a cardiac pathologist when an inherited cause is suspected or the cause of death unexplained.
Toxicology screens are recommended in SD cases with uncertain cause of death.
For SCD where the cause is known or suspected to be heritable, genetic testing targeted to the cause is recommended.

Following SADS, post-mortem genetic testing targeted to primary electrical disease is recommended when the decedent is young (<50 years of age) and/or the circumstances and/or family history support a primary electrical disease.
When an autopsy diagnoses possible heritable cardiac disease, it is recommended to refer first-degree relatives for cardiac assessment in a specialized clinic.
In non-autopsied cases of SD where inherited cardiac disease is suspected, it is recommended to refer first-degree relatives for cardiac assessment in a specialized clinic.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for optimization of device programming

rows.recommendation: Optimization of ICD programming is indicated to avoid inappropriate and unnecessary therapies and to reduce mortality.
In single- or dual-chamber ICD patients without bradycardia pacing indications, it is recommended to minimize ventricular pacing.
Programming of prolonged detection settings is indicated (duration criteria of at least 6–12 s or 30 intervals).
It is recommended to program the slowest tachycardia therapy zone limit ≥188 b.p.m. in primary prevention ICD patients.
In patients with SHD, programming of at least one ATP therapy is recommended in all tachyarrhythmias zones.
It is recommended to program algorithms for SVT vs. VT discrimination for tachycardias with rates up to 230 b.p.m.
It is recommended to activate lead failure alerts.
Remote monitoring is recommended to reduce the incidence of inappropriate shocks.
Programming of burst ATP as a first attempt is recommended over ramp ATP.
For S-ICDs, a dual detection zone configuration is recommended with activation of discrimination algorithm in the lower conditional shock zone.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for risk stratification, sudden cardiac death prevention, and treatment of ventricular arrhythmia in chronic coronary artery disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with syncope and previous STEMI, PES is indicated when syncope remains unexplained after non-invasive evaluation.

ICD implantation is recommended in patients without ongoing ischaemia with documented VF or haemodynamically not-tolerated VT occurring later than 48 h after MI.
In patients with CAD and recurrent, symptomatic SMVT or ICD shocks for SMVT despite chronic amiodarone therapy, catheter ablation is recommended in preference to escalating AAD therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for sudden cardiac death prevention in patients with coronary anomalies

rows.recommendation: Cardiac stress imaging during physical exercise is recommended in addition to cardiopulmonary exercise test in patients with anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery with an interarterial course to confirm/exclude myocardial ischaemia.

Surgery is recommended in patients with anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery with CA, syncope suspected to be due to VAs or angina when other causes have been excluded.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients with idiopathic premature ventricular complexes/ventricular tachycardia

rows.recommendation: Regular assessment of ventricular function of patients with PVC burden >10% and normal ventricular function is indicated.
Catheter ablation as first-line treatment is recommended for symptomatic idiopathic VT/PVCs from the RVOT or the left fascicles.
Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine CCB are indicated in symptomatic patients with idiopathic VT/PVCs from an origin other than the RVOT or the left fascicles.
Catheter ablation is not recommended in children <5 years of age or <10 kg weight except when previous medical therapy fails or when VT is not haemodynamically tolerated.
Amiodarone as a first-line treatment is not recommended in patients with idiopathic VTs/PVCs.
Verapamil is not recommended in children ≤1 year of age with PVC/VT, particularly if they have signs of heart failure or concurrent use of other AADs.

rows.recommendation: In patients with a cardiomyopathy suspected to be caused by frequent and predominately monomorphic PVCs, catheter ablation is recommended.

ICD implantation is recommended in ARVC patients with haemodynamically not-tolerated VT or VF.

In a first-degree relative of a patient with ARVC, ECG, and echocardiogram are recommended.

It is recommended that patients with neuromuscular disorders who have VAs or ventricular dysfunction are treated in the same way for arrhythmia as patients without neuromuscular disorders.
Invasive electrophysiological evaluation is recommended in patients with myotonic dystrophy and palpitations or syncope suggestive of VA, VT, or surviving a CA.

In symptomatic patients with BBR-VT, catheter ablation is recommended.
In patients with myotonic dystrophy undergoing ablation for BBR-VT, pacemaker/ICD implantation is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for sudden cardiac death prevention, and treatment of ventricular arrhythmia in myocarditis

rows.recommendation: In confirmed or clinically suspected acute myocarditis, it is recommended that patients who present with life-threatening VA are referred to a specialized centre.
In patients with haemodynamically not-tolerated SMVT occurring in the chronic phase of myocarditis, an ICD implantation is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for risk stratification, sudden cardiac death prevention, and treatment of ventricular arrhythmia in cardiac sarcoidosis

rows.recommendation: ICD implantation is recommended in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis who have an LVEF <35%.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis who (a) have documented sustained VT, or (2) aborted CA.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for sudden cardiac death prevention, and treatment of ventricular arrhythmia in valvular heart disease

rows.recommendation: PES with standby catheter ablation is recommended in patients with aortic valve disease and SMVT to identify and ablate BBR-VT, especially if it occurs following a valve intervention.

In patients with valvular heart disease and persistent LV dysfunction after surgical correction (if possible) it is recommended that ICD implantation for primary prevention follows DCM/HNDCM recommendations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for sudden cardiac death prevention, and treatment of ventricular arrhythmia in congenital heart disease

rows.recommendation: In adults with CHD with biventricular physiology and a left systemic ventricle presenting with symptomatic heart failure (NYHA II/III) and EF <35% despite ≥3 months of OMT, ICD implantation is indicated.
In patients with CHD presenting with sustained VAs, evaluation for residual or new anatomical abnormalities is recommended.
In patients with CHD with not-tolerated VT/aborted CA due to VF, ICD implantation is indicated after exclusion of reversible causes.
In patients with repaired TOF who present with SMVT or recurrent, symptomatic appropriate ICD therapy for SMVT, catheter ablation performed in specialized centres is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with idiopathic ventricular fibrillation

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that idiopathic VF is diagnosed in a SCA survivor, preferably with documentation of VF, after exclusion of an underlying structural, channelopathic, metabolic, or toxicological aetiology.
ICD implantation is recommended in idiopathic VF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with long QT syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that LQTS is diagnosed with either QTc ≥ 480 ms in repeated 12-lead ECGs with or without symptoms or LQTS diagnostic score >3.
In patients with clinically diagnosed long QT syndrome, genetic testing, and genetic counselling are recommended.
It is recommended that LQTS is diagnosed in the presence of a pathogenic mutation, irrespective of the QT duration.
Routine diagnostic testing with epinephrine challenge is not recommended in LQTS.

The following is recommended in LQTS:
• Avoid QT-prolonging drugs.
• Avoid and correct electrolyte abnormalities.
• Avoid genotype-specific triggers for arrhythmias.
Beta-blockers, ideally non-selective beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol), are recommended in LQTS patients with documented QT interval prolongation, to reduce risk of arrhythmic events.
Mexiletine is indicated in LQT3 patients with a prolonged QT interval.
ICD implantation in addition to beta-blockers is recommended in LQTS patients with CA.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with LQTS who are symptomatic while receiving beta-blockers and genotype-specific therapies.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome

rows.recommendation: Genetic testing is recommended in patients with suspected Andersen–Tawil syndrome.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with Andersen–Tawil syndrome after aborted CA not tolerated sustained VT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with Brugada syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that BrS is diagnosed in patients with no other heart disease and a spontaneous type 1 Brugada ECG pattern.

It is recommended that BrS is diagnosed in patients with no other heart disease who have survived a CA due to VF or PVT and exhibit a type 1 Brugada ECG induced by sodium channel blocker challenge or during fever.
Genetic testing for SCN5A gene is recommended for probands with BrS.
Sodium channel blocker test is not recommended in patients with a prior type I Brugada pattern.

The following is recommended in all patients with BrS: (a) Avoidance of drugs that may induce ST-segment elevation in right precordial leads (http://www.brugadadrugs.org). (b) Avoidance of cocaine, cannabis, and excessive alcohol intake. (c) Treatment of fever with antipyretic drugs.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with BrS who: (a) Are survivors of an aborted CA, and/or (b) Have documented spontaneous sustained VT.
Catheter ablation in asymptomatic BrS patients is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with early repolarization pattern/syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that the ERP is diagnosed as J-point elevation of ≥1 mm in two adjacent inferior and/or lateral ECG leads.
It is recommended that the ERS is diagnosed in a patient resuscitated from unexplained VF/PVT in the presence of ERP.
Clinical evaluation is not recommended routinely in asymptomatic subjects with ERP.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with a diagnosis of ERS who have survived a CA.
ICD implantation is not recommended in asymptomatic patients with an isolated ERP.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that CPVT is diagnosed in the presence of a structurally normal heart, normal ECG, and exercise- or emotion-induced bidirectional or PVT.
It is recommended that CPVT is diagnosed in patients who are carriers of a mutation in disease-causing genes.
Genetic testing and genetic counselling are indicated in patients with clinical suspicion or clinical diagnosis of CPVT.
Avoidance of competitive sports, strenuous exercise, and exposure to stressful environments is recommended in all patients with CPVT.
Beta-blockers, ideally non-selective ( nadolol or propranolol ), are recommended in all patients with a clinical diagnosis of CPVT.
ICD implantation combined with beta-blockers and flecainide is recommended in CPVT patients after aborted CA.
PES is not recommended for stratification of SCD risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with short QT syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that SQTS is diagnosed in the presence of a QTc ≤360 ms and one or more of the following: (a) a pathogenic mutation, (b) a family history of SQTS, (c) survival from a VT/VF episode in the absence of heart disease.
Genetic testing is indicated in patients diagnosed with SQTS.
ICD implantation is recommended in patients with a diagnosis of SQTS who: (a) are survivors of an aborted CA, and/or (b) have documented spontaneous sustained VT.
PES is not recommended for SCD risk stratification in SQTS patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the prevention of sudden cardiac death and management of ventricular arrhythmia during pregnancy

rows.recommendation: During pregnancy, electrical cardioversion is recommended for sustained VT.
If ICD implantation is indicated during pregnancy, implantation is recommended with optimal radiation protection.
Continuation of beta-blockers is recommended during pregnancy and post-partum in patients with LQTS or CPVT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for risk stratification and prevention of sudden cardiac death in athletes

rows.recommendation: In athletes with positive medical history, abnormal physical examination, or ECG alterations, further investigations including echocardiography and/or CMR to confirm (or exclude) an underlying disease are recommended.
It is recommended that athletes diagnosed with a cardiovascular disease associated with SCD are managed according to current guidelines for sports eligibility.
It is recommended that staff at sporting facilities are trained in CPR and in the use of AED.
